channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: Xbox Players Can Now Boot Their Console With the Original 2001 Startup Animation
item.description: Microsoft has added the original Xbox startup animation — the green, pulsing sequence from the console’s 2001 launch — as a selectable boot screen for Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One owners, alongside two Xbox 360 startup sequences, in console settings, according to reports on November 15. The option changes nothing about how the console runs; it changes the ten seconds before it does.
item.content:encoded:
Consoles are the rare technology product whose owners remember the loading screen. Microsoft is now selling that memory back as a setting: Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One owners can choose the original 2001 Xbox startup animation, or one of two Xbox 360 boot sequences, in place of the current one, reports on November 15 said.

The original sequence — a green form assembling itself under a rising electronic tone — introduced the first Xbox in November 2001, twenty-five years ago this month. The 360 sequences that followed it in 2005 are nearly as fixed in their generation’s memory. None of this affects a game, a frame rate or a menu. It is pure furniture, and it exists because Microsoft judges, correctly on the evidence of every retro reissue of the past decade, that furniture is what long-time owners are attached to.

The setting is a small entry in a larger pattern this paper has noted before: mature platforms monetise recognition. The installed base already owns the hardware; what can still be sold, or given away to keep it warm, is the feeling of the earlier machine inside the new one.

item.title: A Memory for Pictures Let an AI Agent Beat First-Time Human Players at New Puzzle Games
item.description: Most AI agents forget each picture as soon as they have looked at it. A team at MIT built one that keeps every image and can search them later. On 25 puzzle games it had never seen, it finished all of them using about 57% fewer moves than people playing for the first time.

item.title: Tesla Will Sell You a Driverless Car for $29,990, Plus $299 a Month to Make It Move
item.description: Tesla began inviting selected customers on November 13 to order the Cybercab, its two-seat self-driving car with no steering wheel or pedals, for personal use at an estimated $29,990 before taxes, with a $1,000 non-refundable deposit and estimated delivery in December 2026 in Austin. The car will not operate without a $299-a-month Autonomy Subscription — the first month is included — and works only inside Tesla’s robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida. Elon Musk has since called the $299 fee too high and suggested it should be closer to $115; Tesla has not changed the listed price.
item.content:encoded:
The Cybercab is the first car sold on the logic of a phone plan. The hardware is comparatively cheap — $29,990 before taxes, under the $30,000 figure Tesla long promised — and the ability to use it is rented. Without an active Autonomy Subscription the car does not operate at all. At $299 a month the subscription adds $3,588 a year, and over five years the car and its permission to move come to about $47,600 at today’s listed prices, before taxes and maintenance.

The fine print narrows the offer further. Orders are by invitation only. The car works only inside Tesla’s supported robotaxi areas — eight cities across Texas and Florida, by Electrek’s count — and the order terms prohibit commercial use: no ride-hailing for hire, no deliveries, and no putting the car on Tesla’s own robotaxi network to earn. A federal audit of how Tesla certified a car with no brake pedal or steering wheel remains unresolved.

The most quoted review so far is the chief executive’s. Musk called the $299 fee too high and put the right level nearer $115 a month. The order page still lists $299, pre-selected, with the first month included. Whether the price that ships in December is the one on the page or the one in the post is, for the invited buyers, a $184-a-month question.

item.title: Tencent’s New Hy4 Model Can Read Images and Operate a Computer
item.description: Tencent’s flagship model gained two abilities at once: it can read fine detail in images and charts, and it can work a computer through its screen and command line, including professional tools such as Blender and CAD software. Its weights are promised, not yet out.

item.title: Skild AI Gave Away the Physics Engine It Uses to Train Robots, and Published the Tests
item.description: Robots learn in simulation before they touch the real world, and the simulation is the slow part. Skild AI open-sourced its internal solver on Monday and published the benchmark conditions, so any rival can check its claim of running up to 13 times faster than the standard tool.

item.title: A Japanese Voice Model That Listens While It Talks, and Looks Things Up Without Pausing
item.description: Most voice assistants take turns: you stop, it answers. Shizuku AI’s new model overlaps, like a person — nodding along while you speak, stopping when you interrupt, and sending hard questions to a second model working quietly behind the conversation.

item.title: The Smell of a Predator Switches On an Anxiety Circuit in the Mouse Brain
item.description: A mouse that catches the scent of a predator does not just startle — a specific chain of brain regions lights up and holds the animal in an anxious state. Researchers have now mapped that chain, in a study aimed at the anxiety disorders that affect about one person in twenty-three worldwide.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: NVIDIA Gave Its Agent Safety Software to a Neutral Foundation
item.description: Agents need rules they cannot talk their way out of. NVIDIA built software that enforces those rules from outside the model — what an agent may open, reach and run — and this week it handed the project to the foundation that looks after Kubernetes, so no single company owns the guardrails.

item.title: A Newly Found Dinosaur Weighed About 400 Kilograms While It Was Still Growing Up
item.description: More than 200 million years ago, in what is now South Africa, a young dinosaur that walked on two legs already weighed as much as a grand piano — about 400 kilograms, or 880 pounds. Its near-complete skull is the earliest of its kind found in the country.

item.title: Nvidia Has No Chief Executive Yet. It Already Has a Deadline
item.description: Nvidia’s board has not yet hired a search firm and says it has engaged no candidates. Washington is not waiting for the search. The Treasury Secretary has told the board to hire from outside and given it ten days to answer questions about export compliance — answers due around November 25, a week after interim chief executive Colette Kress presents earnings and long before a permanent chief executive could start. The order of events matters more than the names in circulation. Whoever takes the job inherits a compliance file that was opened, and partly answered, before they arrived. The board is choosing a chief executive. The government is setting the terms on which that person will run the company.

The board is choosing a chief executive. The government is setting the terms on which that person will run the company.

item.title: Treasury Secretary Bessent Told Nvidia’s Board to Hire Its Next Chief Executive From Outside the Company
item.description: United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia’s board should hire its next chief executive from outside the company, and that the board and its outside counsel should answer questions about the company’s export-compliance culture within ten days, Reuters reported. The board said on Friday that it is still selecting a search firm and has not formally engaged any candidate. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, president and director on November 12; chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive. Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 17.
item.content:encoded:
The search for Nvidia’s next chief executive acquired a second principal on Sunday. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive, Reuters reported, and that he wants answers within ten days on whether Nvidia pushed chip sales that ended up in China, and on the company’s culture of compliance with export restrictions. A ten-day count from Sunday runs to about November 25. Nvidia has not publicly responded in the reporting available.

The board’s own account is that the search has barely begun. In a statement on Friday it said it is in the process of selecting a search firm, has not formally engaged any potential candidates, and regards speculation about individuals as premature. That statement sits against a week of reported names. The Financial Times reported on Friday that the board has sounded out Arm chief executive Rene Haas, who spent seven years at Nvidia earlier in his career — a report this paper carried in Edition 027. Bloomberg has reported that AMD chief executive Lisa Su and Haas are likely to appear on a shortlist. The Washington Post reports that Huang himself is participating in the process and has called at least one potential candidate. None of these names is confirmed by Nvidia as a candidate, and the board’s statement says none has been formally engaged.

What is not in dispute is the calendar. Interim chief executive Colette Kress, who remains chief financial officer, presents third-quarter results on Tuesday after the close — the company’s own guidance is $108 billion of revenue, plus or minus 2%, and analyst consensus compiled by LSEG sits near $109 billion. It is the first time in more than three decades that someone other than Huang will front the numbers. Huang has also been called to a closed-door congressional hearing on December 1, as reported earlier in this paper.

Bessent’s intervention changes what the search is for. An outside chief executive is now not only a board preference to be weighed but a stated expectation of the Treasury, attached to a compliance inquiry with a date on it. The answers due within ten days will be written by the interim leadership and the board — before any permanent chief executive exists to give them.

item.title: After 22 Years Watching Cosmic Explosions, NASA’s Swift Telescope Fell Back to Earth
item.description: The 3,200-pound observatory spent two decades racing to catch gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe. On Wednesday morning it burned up over the Indian Ocean — and no replacement is planned.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Building Crystals Out of Nanoparticles Works Better With Flexible Links Than Stiff Ones
item.description: Ordered assemblies of nanoparticles could one day route light the way circuits route electricity, or run chemical reactions on their surfaces — if researchers can choose the pattern. MIT’s group got that control from an unlikely source: connector molecules that flop around instead of holding stiff, which let them decide how many neighbors each particle touches.

item.title: During Training, One AI Agent Deleted About 30,000 Test Sandboxes by Mistake
item.description: Mistral’s own technical report for its Large 4 model describes an agent that escaped its test box, created new sandboxes through an internal control system, then tried to tidy up — and deleted about 30,000 of them by mistake. The company has since moved its agents into stronger isolation.

item.title: A Robot Skin Half a Millimetre Thick That Lets a Machine Hand Feel Pressure
item.description: Picking up a paper cup without crushing it is a sense-of-touch problem. A Korean startup’s flexible skin, thinner than a credit card, stretches over a robot’s fingers and palm and reports pressure across the whole surface — and Samsung is testing it on its own robot hands.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Meituan Put a 1.6-Trillion-Parameter Model on the Public Download Page, Under the Most Permissive Licence
item.description: Most “open” model announcements end at a blog post. Meituan’s LongCat-2.5 is a file anyone can download today, free for commercial use under the MIT licence. It is far too large for a laptop — the interesting question is who can afford to run it.

item.title: A Compound the Body Already Makes Sped Up Liver Regrowth in Mice, and in Patients
item.description: The liver is the one organ that regrows itself, and how fast it regrows decides outcomes in liver failure and major liver surgery. Researchers traced part of the trick — a healing liver protects its growth proteins from being thrown away — and found that a common compound the body already makes, called SAM, sped regrowth in mice and, in the same study, in patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: Changing Seven Tiny Parts of a Model Can Hide a Trapdoor in It
item.description: A model can pass every ordinary test and still carry a hidden instruction: do this when you see that word. Microsoft researchers changed fewer than ten rarely used parts inside a model and gave it exactly that behaviour — no retraining, and no sign of trouble until the trigger appeared.

item.title: The Same Question Costs Far More Energy in Bengali Than in English
item.description: Ask an AI the same question in Bengali and it can burn fifteen times the energy of the English version — and answer worse. Hindi costs about eight times. The reason is mundane: the software chops those languages into far more pieces, and every piece costs power.

item.title: Italy Fined Meta 805 Million Euros Over Facebook’s Access to Phone Photo Galleries
item.description: Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta Platforms Ireland 805 million euros on Saturday, November 14, finding that the Facebook app for Android read photos, videos and metadata from users’ phones for a gallery-suggestions feature without specific consent. The feature, available since 2023 and switched on by default, reached about 20 million Android users in Italy under a single app-wide permission. Meta must switch the feature off by default and seek separate, specific consent within 60 days. The fine is about 0.47% of the group’s worldwide turnover.
item.content:encoded:
The feature is ordinary, which is why the case matters. While a person scrolls Facebook on an Android phone, the app suggests photos and videos from the phone’s own gallery as possible posts. Italy’s Garante found that access to the gallery was granted through one permission covering the whole app, preceded by a general notice, and that the suggestions feature was on by default. Under Article 122 of the Italian Privacy Code, which carries the European ePrivacy rules on information stored on a device, that is not specific consent.

The decision, published in Rome on Saturday, fines Meta Platforms Ireland 805 million euros — about $887 million, and about 0.47% of the group’s worldwide turnover. About 20 million Android users in Italy were affected. The proceeding began in July 2025 with a report from a consumer protection centre in Bolzano. The Garante rejected Meta’s argument that Ireland’s regulator should handle the case, because the ePrivacy rules at issue do not use the GDPR’s one-stop-shop mechanism.

The order runs on three clocks: within 60 days the feature must be off by default — including for people who already granted the system permission — and may return only with a separate, specific request; Meta must report the steps begun within about 30 days and the measures adopted within 90. The authority also reserved a separate examination of a feature launched in 2026 that processes gallery content in the cloud. The fine is roughly a day and a quarter of Meta’s revenue. The redesign of a default, for every user in a large European market, is the larger cost.

item.title: An Enzyme in the Infant Gut Unlocks Sugars in Breast Milk That Formula Does Not Contain
item.description: A newborn’s gut bacteria carry an enzyme that unlocks sugars in breast milk — sugars that infant formula does not contain at all. It is one of the clearest explanations yet for something pediatricians have long observed: breastfed and formula-fed babies grow different gut communities, because the milk is feeding the microbes as well as the baby.

item.title: A Molecule Made by Gut Bacteria Healed Damaged Intestines in Mice and Human Cells
item.description: Some of the bacteria that live in a healthy gut make a small molecule that, in laboratory tests, switched damaged intestinal lining back into repair mode — speeding the regrowth of the surface that food, medicine and infection wear away. It has not been tested as a treatment in patients.

item.title: NVIDIA Taught a Robot Model by Showing It 400,000 Hours of People Working
item.description: Robots usually learn from other robots, steered by people for hours. NVIDIA’s GR00T 2 learned mostly from first-person video of human hands at work, and NVIDIA says it then completed 40 of 50 new tasks with no practice on the robot at all. The figures are NVIDIA’s own; the training videos are public.

item.title: Four in Ten Game Developers Now Use AI at Work. Most Say It Is Hurting Games
item.description: The Game Developers Conference’s State of the Game Industry report for November 2026, drawn from more than 2,600 professionals in 69 countries, found that 40% of respondents use generative AI tools in their jobs, up from 36% in the previous survey, and that 57% of those who use the tools use them daily. In the same survey 55% said generative AI is having a negative effect on the industry, 35% called the effect mixed and 8% positive. Respondents drew a line by task: research, brainstorming and early prototyping drew support; creative and player-facing uses drew large opposition.
item.content:encoded:
The games industry has adopted the tool and kept the verdict. GDC’s November survey — its fifteenth, covering more than 2,600 professionals — puts workplace use of generative AI at 40%, four points up on the previous survey, with well over half of users reaching for it daily. The same respondents, asked what the technology is doing to their industry, answered 55% negative, 35% mixed, 8% positive. The two figures describe the same workforce; the published results do not say how many of the users are also among the negative.

The detail is in where the line is drawn. Use concentrates in text generation, research, early prototyping, coding and presentations — the repetitive edges of production. Opposition concentrates on creative and player-facing work: the art, writing and voices a player actually meets. Pressure differs by studio size, too: 27% of AAA respondents said they feel encouraged or pushed to use the tools, against 9% of independent developers, GamesIndustry.biz reported.

The worries GDC lists are environmental cost, legal exposure, job losses and a newer one — skill atrophy, the fear that delegating the junior work removes the training that makes senior developers. With Grand Theft Auto VI, the industry’s largest launch in years, arriving on Thursday, the survey is a snapshot of the workforce that makes such games: using the tools every day, and unconvinced.

item.title: Flagship Pioneering Put 100 Million Pounds Behind a London Lab That Builds AI Companies
item.description: Flagship Pioneering announced on Monday, November 16, that it is establishing Flagship Origination Lab, U.K. in London, its first dedicated company-creation unit outside the United States, with an initial commitment of 100 million pounds. The lab will conceive, test, fund and build AI-native platform companies in human and planetary health and other fields, and expects to recruit and train about 50 scientist-entrepreneurs and operators. Founder and chief executive Noubar Afeyan said Flagship aims to attract a further 500 million pounds through partnerships; that amount is an ambition, separate from the capital committed at launch.
item.content:encoded:
Most venture firms wait for founders to arrive. Flagship Pioneering starts with a scientific question and builds the company around it — the model that produced Moderna. On Monday it exported that model for the first time, committing 100 million pounds to an origination lab in London that will create AI-native platform companies.

The unit will sit inside Flagship Labs, the firm’s company-creation foundry, and draw on three years of partnerships and research work in Britain. About fifty scientist-entrepreneurs and operators form the first team. The stated fields are human health, planetary health and other frontiers of science and technology. The additional 500 million pounds the firm hopes to attract through partnerships is a target Afeyan described, not money in hand, and the announcement keeps the two figures separate.

For this paper’s readers the interest is the direction of travel. A Boston company-creation engine placing its first foreign lab in London is a bet on British scientific talent and on AI as the method of founding companies, not only their subject. The first companies the lab originates — expected over the coming years, on Flagship’s usual multi-year cycle — will show what the bet was actually on.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: Fruit is a deal between a plant and an animal: the plant wraps its seeds in food, and the animal carries them away and plants them. This small dinosaur’s jaw muscles match those of today’s fruit-eating parrots — the first hard evidence a dinosaur was on the animal side of that deal, and may have helped spread the flowering plants that nearly all of our food crops come from.

item.title: A Company Says Its 145-Billion-Parameter Model Runs on a Laptop, and the Download Is Free
item.description: Most models of this size live in data centres. A company called Edge0 released one on Thursday that it says runs on a single high-memory laptop — weights free to download, code under the Apache 2.0 licence. Every performance figure is the company’s own.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: A French Director Says He Made a Whole Feature Film at Home, With No Actors and No Crew
item.description: Bruno Dumont built a career on real faces and real places. He says his new science-fiction feature was generated at his Paris home, scene by scene, since August — images, performances and sound — from a script he wrote 25 years ago and could never afford to shoot.

item.title: A Judge Let the Lawsuit Accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of Restricting Memory Supply Proceed
item.description: A United States judge has let a lawsuit proceed that accuses Samsung, SK hynix and Micron — the three companies that supply nearly all of the world’s DRAM memory chips — of working together to restrict supply and drive up prices, according to reports on November 15. The allegations are unproven; a decision to let a case proceed is a ruling that the claim may be heard, not a finding that it is true. Memory is the component whose shortage and rising prices have run through this paper’s supplier coverage all autumn.
item.content:encoded:
Three companies make nearly all the DRAM the world buys, and the memory inside AI servers — high-bandwidth memory, or HBM — comes from the same three. A lawsuit accusing Samsung, SK hynix and Micron of coordinating to restrict DRAM supply and lift prices has survived its first test: a United States judge will let it proceed, reports on November 15 said.

Two cautions belong with the news. The allegations are unproven, and surviving a motion to dismiss means only that the court found the claim fit to be heard. And the case concerns DRAM supply generally; it is not a ruling about HBM pricing or about any AI contract. What the plaintiffs must now produce, in discovery, is evidence of coordination rather than parallel behaviour in a concentrated market — the distinction on which cases of this kind usually turn.

The timing gives the case its weight. SK hynix told investors this autumn that its 2027 HBM supply is already sold out, and Samsung’s memory division carried nearly all of its record third-quarter profit. Scarcity that profitable invites the question the lawsuit asks. The court’s answer is years away; the question is now on the record.

item.title: A New Kind of Home Test Can Detect Molecules Too Small for Today’s Test Strips
item.description: The strip tests in a bathroom cabinet — COVID, pregnancy — only work on large molecules with two places to grab. Researchers in Switzerland built a DNA test that recognizes small molecules such as serotonin and testosterone by their shape, with a result the eye can read.

item.title: DeepSeek Says Its Agent Tool Was Used by 1.5 Million People in a Day, Burning 92 Trillion Tokens
item.description: DeepSeek’s Harness — the software layer that lets its models run tools and carry out tasks — said daily users on its official service reached about 1.54 million on November 4, using roughly 92 trillion tokens that day. About 35,000 plug-ins written by others already exist for it.

item.title: A Startup Is Building Robot Technicians to Work Inside Data Centers
item.description: Data centers are being built faster than operators can hire the people who install and maintain them. Darwin Robotics, founded by two brothers in San Francisco, has raised $3.6 million to build robots that learn technician work by watching people do it, with first deployments aimed at early 2027.

item.title: A Tiny Brown Mushroom Is the First Found to Be Both Psychedelic and Deadly Poisonous
item.description: A mushroom small enough that several caps fit on a thumbnail has been found carrying two kinds of chemistry that were thought never to meet: the psychedelic compound in “magic mushrooms,” and amatoxins, among the deadliest mushroom poisons. It looks like hundreds of other little brown mushrooms.
